title: Pride in the album; why she doesn't perform it live
summary: She can't improve on it but won't play it for audiences who swing it, and recalls Dick Hyman's declaiming at a presentation.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: I like them all. From listening to my own records or albums sometimes, I sort of feel like we could've done it, or I could've done it better than that.
But I don't see how I could've done these any better than I did -- we do work a little harder (inaudible).
I don't play it very often because I don't want to get a big head.

And what really distresses me, is the fact that I don't get a chance to do these in -- I don't include them in my repertoire when I'm doing personal appearances, because I don't feel that I have enough time to work with ever who is going to be accompanying me to give it the proper flavor.
Because they would have a tendency to swing it too much, and it would take away.
Sure.
You absolutely couldn't afford to be haphazard about --

I thought when we recorded these, there would an opportunity for Dick and I to work together, you know, on different engagements so that I could get a feel of the reaction from the audience. And then, too, I would become more familiar and more comfortable by doing them in front of an audience. I tried to do -- I did try to do 'Take Oh Take Those Lips Away,' which, as I said before, is a very beautiful ballad. But it got to be -- You know, at the end, there is a spot where I repeat the ending, and then there is a -- The last time I repeated it, there is a big pause there with nothing happening. And then there is, of course, sort of a surprise ending. What disturbed me, it got to me a gimmick. You know, that's all they were waiting for --

the ending of this song. They weren't listening to the ballad at all.
So, I have not included it in my repertoire.
We did get a chance to do these things -- Dick and I -- all of them, at one of the Overseas Press Club's jazz parties.
And it was with just Dick on piano, and they (inaudible) bit of it. The only thing about it, we had Earl Hyman who is a Shakespeare actor.
He was the declaiming all over the place --
What was his role? He'd do commentary) in between the songs?
Yes, that's what he was supposed to do. But instead of him more or less introducing them, he would practically recite the lyrics, you know, before I sang them.
I mean, a real Shakespearean actor would do which --
You know, there's some controversy. I mean, did these people really act like that? I mean,
